In practice, intelligibility requires at least three tiers. Capability transparency would parallel the force-structure declarations already made under the Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (START). It presents the fewest political obstacles because that precedent exists. States have a disclosure mechanism, verification methods and the political cover to use them. Constraint and causal-logic transparency enjoy no comparable scaffolding, which is why both are harder to negotiate. Constraint transparency means visibility into what the system is programmed not to recommend. It has no precedent in nuclear arms control. Yet it is the tier most relevant to escalation opacity, because it answers the question adversaries actually need answered: what your system will not do in a crisis. Causal-logic transparency – how specific inputs produce specific outputs – is maximally invasive and probably unachievable in the near term, but even partial progress would reduce the opacity that fuels adversarial anxiety.

Haleema Saadia and her colleagues have proposed an arms-control framework specific-ally for AI and nuclear decisions that begins to address this requirement. Alexey Arbatov’s analysis of Russian strategic-stability perspectives confirms that
concern about temporal compression is shared among adversaries and is not merely a unilateral Western worry
. At the same time, Anna Nadibaidze and Nicolò Miotto have shown that US and Russian discourses on AI and strategic stability are diverging in ways that compound the opacity problem.

To ameliorate it, three governance mechanisms appear to be required. Algorithmic verification channels would function as software-mediated hotlines – secure pathways for querying adversary decision constraints during crises, receiving cryptographically verified responses without full algorithmic disclosure. The model extends the rationale for the 1963 hotline and the 1987 Nuclear Risk Reduction Centers. Anna Péczeli’s analysis suggests such channels need multilateral architectures, not merely bilateral ones. Technical confidence-building measures – including code-freeze periods and joint auditing of the conditions under which AI systems produce false positives – would extend the Helsinki precedent from physical force movements to algorithmic behaviours. And human-override doctrine would require that human authority be architecturally enforced: hardcoded as physically impossible to bypass, not just procedurally mandated through policies that software updates could modify. Existing nuclear doctrine mandates human authorisation for release. It does not physically prevent automated systems from preparing and queuing release sequences in ways that make human reversal operationally costly.
The gap between procedural mandate and structural impossibility is where control goes to die.
